content: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is frequently identified through the presence of elevated urinary albumin excretion, known as albuminuria, or a reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), both of which are markers of kidney damage. Diabetic kidney disease, a specific subtype of CKD caused by diabetes, affects approximately 20-40% of adults with diabetes. This condition typically develops within 10 to 20 years following the onset of diabetes. However, in individuals with type 2 diabetes, CKD may already be present at the time of diabetes diagnosis. The progression of CKD in individuals with diabetes significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular complications and leads to higher healthcare costs. In its severe stages, CKD can progress to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), a condition that necessitates either dialysis or kidney transplantation for survival.
